content_html:
DishwasherBench is a dishwasher-loading game on a physical simulation of a real machine, built to benchmark language models and playable by people in a browser. The game inside is called Spotless, and the packages are named @spotless/*.

A player loads a 3D model of a Bosch SMV4HAX40G with rigid-body physics. A wash on its Eco 50 programme is then simulated (jets, droplets, run-off, soil and detergent chemistry), and the player gets points for every item that comes out clean. On every level after the first, not everything fits, so the player has to choose what to load and how.

  • Physical. Loading is rigid-body physics on exact shapes. The wash traces water from the nozzle positions measured on the machine and is calibrated on a test wash of it.
  • Deterministic and verifiable. The same load always settles the same way, and every episode is a record that anyone can verify by replaying it and by washing its load again.
  • One game for people and models. People play in a browser and models play through MCP, with the same actions on the same grid.

Built and maintained by Composo.

Loading the first level in the browser. A dinner plate is in hand over the lower basket, and "Suggest spots" has numbered the free seats, best first. The panel on the right holds the exact pose a program would send.

Features

  • The machine. A Bosch SMV4HAX40G as data and geometry, from photographs and tape readings of the real machine (packages/machine): both baskets with their tine rows, shelves and rests, the spray arms and the Eco 50 programme.
  • Loading. A catalogue of items and soils, deterministic rigid-body loading (Jolt), and a session layer with the actions and queries of the game (place, remove, set_rack, list_slots, check_load and the rest).
  • The wash. A simulation at two tiers: the official tier gives the scored result, and the fast tier a preview in about a minute. An official wash of the largest level takes about five minutes on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Pro).
  • A course of seven levels, numbered in order of difficulty (docs/benchmark/levels.md), each with saved reference loads of three scripted players (careful, careless, random).
  • Three ways to play. The page (apps/web), an MCP server for agents (packages/mcp), and a harness that runs scripted players and models and writes verified episode records (packages/bench).
  • Checks. 48 loading phenomena from the literature as executable pairs of washes (docs/research/standards.md section 9), and a calibration tool that scores the simulation against a record of a real wash, fits parameters and ranks candidate test washes.

Requirements

  • macOS. Developed and tested on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Pro, 18 GB) under macOS 27, where every figure in this repository was measured. Linux and Windows are untested (issue 28).
  • Node 20.19 or newer in the 20 line (.nvmrc pins 20.19.0; an older Node is refused at install), and pnpm 9 (package.json names 9.4.0; corepack enable picks it up).
  • A GPU that Dawn can open. The wash traces water on the GPU through WebGPU from Node (the webgpu package, version 0.6.2, which carries prebuilt Dawn binaries). On a Mac that is Metal. Version 0.6.2 loads on macOS 27 and does not load on macOS 14.7.
  • Google Chrome or Chromium, for the pictures an agent is sent and for the scripts that drive the page. The harness looks for it in the usual install locations; set SPOTLESS_CHROME to the path of the program to choose another. Playing by hand needs only a desktop browser, and scripted players need none (--no-render).
  • Disk and memory. About 680 MB for the clone (a download of about 290 MB) and about 420 MB for node_modules; 1 to 2 GB of memory for an official wash of a level.
  • Ports 8787 (game server) and 8788 (MCP server), or others of your choosing.

Results are repeatable bit for bit on one machine, and every result names the stack it was computed on: across machines, operating-system builds and versions of the webgpu package, results can differ in the last bits (docs/research/spike-gpu-compute-macos27-recheck.md).

Quick start

git clone https://github.com/composo-ai/DishwasherBench.git
cd DishwasherBench
corepack enable                       # once: makes pnpm 9.4.0 available
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile        # about 15 seconds the first time

There is no build step for the packages: they are consumed as TypeScript source and run with tsx. Only the page is built, by the play command below.

Wash a saved load from the command line:

pnpm --filter @spotless/wash-runner wash-load tutorial-careful --tier fast       # under a minute
pnpm --filter @spotless/wash-runner wash-load tutorial-careful --tier official   # about 5 minutes the first time

It prints the points and, for each item, the verdict, the score and what is left on it. The saved loads are in packages/loader/loads/ (<level>-<player>.json). The first wash of a load works out where the water goes and keeps that in .spotless/exposure-cache, so a second wash of the same load takes seconds to about a minute (pass --no-cache to switch this off).

Run the checks:

pnpm typecheck      # the root and every package; a few seconds
pnpm test           # every package; 8 to 17 minutes, with real washes on the GPU

A wash is tied to its parameter set. The set the game washes with (anchored-v7.owner-capsule, in packages/calibration/anchors/) records the state of the simulation source and of the machine data it was made for. After a change to either, the wash stops and lists what differs. CONTRIBUTING.md explains the rule and how to make the set current again.

Play in the browser

pnpm --filter @spotless/web play

This builds the page and starts the game server. Open http://127.0.0.1:8787 (add --port <n> for another port). The page plays music; the Sound button turns it off.

When you start the wash you choose between two kinds:

  • Quick preview: the fast tier, in about a minute.
  • Full wash: the official tier, in several minutes. This is the scored result, and the report of a preview offers it on the same load.

The game is scored on Eco 50 with one capsule of detergent (Finish Powerball Ultimate, 12.9 g). The levels are listed 1 to 7 in order of difficulty.

Plates, bowls and cutlery are placed by pointing. For a tight spot, such as a plate beside one already placed or a cup against the side rests of the upper basket, pick the piece up and press "Suggest spots" (it costs one query), then click a numbered mark.

The server answers the page it serves and clients on your own machine. --allow-origin admits a page served from another origin, and --allow-host a request under another host name (SECURITY.md).

After a quick preview of a deliberately careless load of the first level: a bowl left mouth up holds 432 ml of water and is not clean, and the report says that a fork held the lower spray arm still.

Looking closely at one item after the wash: the residue is painted where it was left, with its area and the water the item held.

Run a scripted player

A scripted player needs no model and costs nothing. This plays the first level with the careful reference player at the official tier, then verifies the record by replaying its actions and by washing the load a second time (about five minutes each):

pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies careful \
  --no-render --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/scripted"
pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench verify \
  "$PWD"/.spotless/bench/scripted/tutorial__careful__*/record.json --rewash
  • Give --out as an absolute path; a relative one resolves inside packages/bench.
  • The scripted players are empty, random, careless and careful. Add --tier fast for a preview in about a minute; the record and the results table label it as a preview.
  • Each run writes under --out: record.json, a results table (results.md, results.json), the data of the game server it started (server-data/) and, without --no-render, the pictures the tools returned.

The scripted careful player's load of the largest level (62 pieces on the counter, 49 loaded), from above and from the front and side. Both models that have played beat it.

Run a model

Everything about the harness, what each kind of player sees and what is recorded is in docs/benchmark/README.md.

A model run costs money. Copy .env.example to .env (which git ignores) and fill in the address and the key of your endpoint. The command prints the names of the variables it set, never a value, and neither the key nor the address is written to a record.

A model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenAI, Azure, or any server with the Responses or chat completions API):

pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies openai:gpt-6.1-sol \
  --max-input-tokens 2000000 --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/sol-tutorial"
  • The policy names the model or, on Azure, the deployment: openai:<model or deployment>.
  • --max-input-tokens ends an episode before its requests add up to more. The first level takes 0.4 to 0.65 million input tokens, a level of 37 pieces 2.5 to 2.8 million, and the largest level (62 pieces) 3.0 to 3.2 million, with 95 % or more of it read from the provider's cache. Use limits of 2,000,000, 12,000,000 and 20,000,000.
  • The harness records tokens, and a cost when prices are given in .env.
  • The wash is at the official tier, which is the score; --tier fast gives a preview.
  • Each run writes the record, the transcript, the pictures and a results table under --out, and verifies the episode by replaying its action log.
  • With no address set, no request is made and the command exits with status 1.

A model through Anthropic's API, with the key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (put the model's id in place of <model id>):

pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies anthropic:<model id> \
  --max-input-tokens 2000000 --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/anthropic-tutorial"

The SDK also accepts a stored login profile, so a run can spend without a key in .env.

Connect an MCP client

Any agent that speaks MCP can play. An MCP server is bound to one episode, so start the game server in benchmark mode and create the episode first.

# 1. The game server (the token: 8 characters or more, of your choosing)
pnpm --filter @spotless/server exec tsx src/cli.ts serve --admin-token <token> --wash-tier fast \
  --data "$PWD/.spotless"

# 2. An episode; prints an address for the page, and the episode's id
pnpm --filter @spotless/server exec tsx src/cli.ts link --admin-token <token> \
  --level tutorial --player my-agent --agent

# 3. For a client that speaks streamable HTTP: serves http://127.0.0.1:8788/mcp
pnpm --filter @spotless/mcp exec tsx src/cli.ts --server http://127.0.0.1:8787 \
  --session <episode id> --http --port 8788

--data keeps the server's files, the episode records among them (.spotless/episodes/), in the directory the page uses; without it serve writes to packages/server/.spotless. The address that link prints shows the episode in the page once the page has been built (pnpm --filter @spotless/web build, which play also does). If the game server is on another port (serve --port <n>), give link its address with --server http://127.0.0.1:<n>. For a desktop client that starts the MCP server itself over stdio, the configuration is in docs/benchmark/README.md section 3.

The agent gets thirteen tools (place, remove, reset, set_rack, start_cycle, get_level, get_item, get_state, render, preview, list_slots, check_load, get_report). To try one call by hand:

pnpm --filter @spotless/mcp exec tsx scripts/call.ts --url http://127.0.0.1:8788/mcp get_state '{}'

Both servers listen on 127.0.0.1 and serve clients on your own machine. For a client that reaches them under another name, for example from a container, start them with --allow-host <name> (SECURITY.md).

Results

Two models have played three levels of the course at the official tier, through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint: six episodes, and each figure is a single episode. Points, with the share of the level's points. The middle columns are the scripted reference players.

# Level Points on offer Random Careless Careful gpt-6.1-sol gpt-6-astra
1 tutorial (12 pieces) 64 20 (31.3 %) 58 (90.6 %) 64 (100 %) 64 (100 %) not run
4 breakfast (37) 220 36 (16.4 %) 112 (50.9 %) 174 (79.1 %) 190 (86.4 %); a second episode 188 (85.5 %) 175 (79.5 %)
7 dinner-party (62) 367 88 (24.0 %) 100 (27.2 %) 250 (68.1 %) 260 (70.8 %) 274 (74.7 %)

gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6-astra are the names of the two deployments on the Azure endpoint used; both ran at medium reasoning effort. The three scripted columns are the saved reference loads (docs/benchmark/course-table.md).

  • Both models beat the careful reference load on both full levels, by placing pans, a platter and boards that the scripted player never tries.
  • Neither model made the mistake the levels are built around. No hollow piece was stood mouth up or laid on its side in six episodes, and what the models loaded came out 84 to 100 % clean. Their scores differ by what they fitted in.

The records, transcripts and pictures of the six episodes, and a fuller account, are in docs/benchmark/first-runs/course/. Each episode verifies by replay and by a second wash with the same verdicts and points. Scope and limitations says what decides a score.

How it works

Loading. Every item and every part of the machine is a rigid compound of exact shapes generated from a parametric description; the picture, the collision shape and the surfaces the wash sees all come from that one description. Items are placed with rigid-body physics (Jolt) at a fixed step, with the player's inputs rounded to 1 mm and 1 degree, so that a person and a model act on the same grid and the same load always settles the same way. Every action is logged with a hash of the scene after it, and replaying the log must reproduce every hash. See docs/design/platform.md.

The wash. Jets are traced on the GPU from the nozzle positions measured on the machine and the turning of the arms, onto the exact shapes of the load. Splash and drips travel as droplets; water that lands runs down surfaces as a film, pools where a surface holds it and drains where it does not. A soil model per kind of soil then removes soil with time, temperature and the chemistry of the wash water (detergent, enzymes, bleach), over the whole programme. Where the water goes is cached apart from the soil and the chemistry, so a wash with other soil parameters replays in seconds to about a minute. The official tier works on blocks of 2 mm, the fast tier on 4 mm. See docs/design/scope.md for what is built and what is left out, and docs/design/sim-core.md for the design of the physics.

The scoring. After the wash an inspector looks at every item. An item is clean when it carries at most 4 specks and 4 mm² of visible soil, counting what dirty water left where it stood on the item. Each item is worth a number of points stated on the level card; a clean item earns them, an item that is not clean or was left on the counter earns nothing. An episode is one load and one wash. The report also gives a graded score from 0 to 5 for each item and what is left where, which do not change the points. See docs/benchmark/README.md and docs/benchmark/levels.md.

The calibration. Every physical constant of the wash is in a parameter registry with a default, a range and a source. A wash record describes a real test wash: the machine and the programme, each item with its soil and where it stood, and what was seen afterwards. The calibration tool runs the simulation on a record, scores it against what was seen, fits chosen parameters and says which parameters the data can and cannot identify. The first wash record is four egg-yolk plates on Eco 50. See docs/calibration/wash-record.md, docs/calibration/fitting.md and, for the set the game washes with, docs/calibration/anchoring-v7.md.

Check the simulation yourself

The phenomena suite (48 phenomena, 82 washes; about 15 minutes at the fast tier when nothing is cached, two and a half when everything is). Run these from the root of the repository, in a POSIX shell:

INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts --list
INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts P01 P36 --tier fast \
  --out .spotless/phenomena
INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts P36 --tier fast \
  --params packages/calibration/anchors/anchored-v7.owner-capsule.json --dose-g 12.9 \
  --out .spotless/phenomena

With no ids it runs all 48. Without --params it washes with the registry defaults and the reference detergent; the third form washes as the game does, with the calibrated set and the capsule. The commands above send their reports to the git-ignored .spotless/phenomena. The default is packages/sim-verify/phenomena/reports/, which holds the stored reports of the project.

The calibration tool, on the first test wash:

pnpm --filter @spotless/calibration spotless-fit validate \
  packages/calibration/records/owner/owner-wash-01-egg-yolk-eco50.measured.json
pnpm --filter @spotless/calibration spotless-fit predict \
  packages/calibration/records/owner/owner-wash-01-egg-yolk-eco50.measured.json \
  --params packages/calibration/anchors/anchored-v7.owner-capsule.json

validate checks a wash record; predict says what the simulation gives for every observation in it (five to seven minutes the first time, less once the water of the load is cached). With --params, predict washes as the game does; without it, it uses the registry defaults. Its warning that there is no calibration.json beside the set is expected.

The saved loads against the loading physics:

pnpm --filter @spotless/loader check-loads tutorial-careful
pnpm --filter @spotless/loader check-loads --jobs 3      # all 25 of them: about 50 minutes

Scope and limitations

DishwasherBench models one machine and scores one programme, Eco 50, with one detergent. The wash is calibrated on a test wash of that machine (four egg-yolk plates) and on the published class means of a sister machine, the Bosch SMV6ECX51E. docs/validation/README.md has the full account, with every number and where it comes from.

Three things decide most of a score:

  • What is loaded. An item left on the counter earns nothing.
  • Which way up the hollow pieces go. A glass, mug or pot left mouth up comes out not clean. About three quarters of the gap between a careful and a careless reference load is hollow pieces put in the wrong way up.
  • Detergent and nesting. A blocked detergent tray leaves protein soils (egg, yoghurt, mince, milk) on the load, and a bowl or spoon that lies fully in another comes out not clean.

The wash does not respond to how plates and cutlery are stacked: plates that lean on each other and cutlery crowded into one cell come out clean, where a real machine would be expected to leave soil. A score therefore does not show how well plates and cutlery were stacked (issue 1). Of the 48 loading phenomena in the suite, 17 pass. Drying, spots and film on glass, items moved by the jets and soil settling on clean pieces are outside the model (issue 7). The adapter for Anthropic's API is tested against a local stand-in only (issue 13).

Open work is tracked as issues, each written as something a contributor could pick up, and docs/ROADMAP.md is the map of them.

Contributing

Bug reports, results that look physically wrong, test washes of a real machine, new levels, model results with their episode records and reports from other platforms are all welcome. CONTRIBUTING.md says how to set up, which checks to run before a pull request, and the rule for changing the simulation's source, which is fingerprinted. Please read the code of conduct.

Questions go to the question form among the issue forms. Anything private goes to support@composo.ai; to report a security problem, or something in a photograph or a record that should not be public, see SECURITY.md. What each version contains is in CHANGELOG.md.

This plays the first level with the careful reference player at the official tier, then verifies the record by replaying its actions and by washing the load a second time (about five minutes each): pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies careful \ --no-render --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/scripted" pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench verify \ "$PWD"/.spotless/bench/scripted/tutorial__careful__*/record.json --rewash Give --out as an absolute path; a relative one resolves inside packages/bench. The scripted players are empty, random, careless and careful. Add --tier fast for a preview in about a minute; the record and the results table label it as a preview. Each run writes under --out: record.json, a results table (results.md, results.json), the data of the game server it started (server-data/) and, without --no-render, the pictures the tools returned. The scripted careful player's load of the largest level (62 pieces on the counter, 49 loaded), from above and from the front and side. Both models that have played beat it. Run a model Everything about the harness, what each kind of player sees and what is recorded is in docs/benchmark/README.md. A model run costs money. Copy .env.example to .env (which git ignores) and fill in the address and the key of your endpoint. The command prints the names of the variables it set, never a value, and neither the key nor the address is written to a record. A model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenAI, Azure, or any server with the Responses or chat completions API): pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies openai:gpt-6.1-sol \ --max-input-tokens 2000000 --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/sol-tutorial" The policy names the model or, on Azure, the deployment: openai:<model or deployment>. --max-input-tokens ends an episode before its requests add up to more. The first level takes 0.4 to 0.65 million input tokens, a level of 37 pieces 2.5 to 2.8 million, and the largest level (62 pieces) 3.0 to 3.2 million, with 95 % or more of it read from the provider's cache. Use limits of 2,000,000, 12,000,000 and 20,000,000. The harness records tokens, and a cost when prices are given in .env. The wash is at the official tier, which is the score; --tier fast gives a preview. Each run writes the record, the transcript, the pictures and a results table under --out, and verifies the episode by replaying its action log. With no address set, no request is made and the command exits with status 1. A model through Anthropic's API, with the key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (put the model's id in place of <model id>): pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies anthropic:<model id> \ --max-input-tokens 2000000 --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/anthropic-tutorial" The SDK also accepts a stored login profile, so a run can spend without a key in .env. Connect an MCP client Any agent that speaks MCP can play. An MCP server is bound to one episode, so start the game server in benchmark mode and create the episode first. # 1. The game server (the token: 8 characters or more, of your choosing) pnpm --filter @spotless/server exec tsx src/cli.ts serve --admin-token <token> --wash-tier fast \ --data "$PWD/.spotless" # 2. An episode; prints an address for the page, and the episode's id pnpm --filter @spotless/server exec tsx src/cli.ts link --admin-token <token> \ --level tutorial --player my-agent --agent # 3. For a client that speaks streamable HTTP: serves http://127.0.0.1:8788/mcp pnpm --filter @spotless/mcp exec tsx src/cli.ts --server http://127.0.0.1:8787 \ --session <episode id> --http --port 8788 --data keeps the server's files, the episode records among them (.spotless/episodes/), in the directory the page uses; without it serve writes to packages/server/.spotless. The address that link prints shows the episode in the page once the page has been built (pnpm --filter @spotless/web build, which play also does). If the game server is on another port (serve --port <n>), give link its address with --server http://127.0.0.1:<n>. For a desktop client that starts the MCP server itself over stdio, the configuration is in docs/benchmark/README.md section 3. The agent gets thirteen tools (place, remove, reset, set_rack, start_cycle, get_level, get_item, get_state, render, preview, list_slots, check_load, get_report). To try one call by hand: pnpm --filter @spotless/mcp exec tsx scripts/call.ts --url http://127.0.0.1:8788/mcp get_state '{}' Both servers listen on 127.0.0.1 and serve clients on your own machine. For a client that reaches them under another name, for example from a container, start them with --allow-host <name> (SECURITY.md). Results Two models have played three levels of the course at the official tier, through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint: six episodes, and each figure is a single episode. Points, with the share of the level's points. The middle columns are the scripted reference players. # Level Points on offer Random Careless Careful gpt-6.1-sol gpt-6-astra 1 tutorial (12 pieces) 64 20 (31.3 %) 58 (90.6 %) 64 (100 %) 64 (100 %) not run 4 breakfast (37) 220 36 (16.4 %) 112 (50.9 %) 174 (79.1 %) 190 (86.4 %); a second episode 188 (85.5 %) 175 (79.5 %) 7 dinner-party (62) 367 88 (24.0 %) 100 (27.2 %) 250 (68.1 %) 260 (70.8 %) 274 (74.7 %) gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6-astra are the names of the two deployments on the Azure endpoint used; both ran at medium reasoning effort. The three scripted columns are the saved reference loads (docs/benchmark/course-table.md). Both models beat the careful reference load on both full levels, by placing pans, a platter and boards that the scripted player never tries. Neither model made the mistake the levels are built around. No hollow piece was stood mouth up or laid on its side in six episodes, and what the models loaded came out 84 to 100 % clean. Their scores differ by what they fitted in. The records, transcripts and pictures of the six episodes, and a fuller account, are in docs/benchmark/first-runs/course/. Each episode verifies by replay and by a second wash with the same verdicts and points. Scope and limitations says what decides a score. How it works Loading. Every item and every part of the machine is a rigid compound of exact shapes generated from a parametric description; the picture, the collision shape and the surfaces the wash sees all come from that one description. Items are placed with rigid-body physics (Jolt) at a fixed step, with the player's inputs rounded to 1 mm and 1 degree, so that a person and a model act on the same grid and the same load always settles the same way. Every action is logged with a hash of the scene after it, and replaying the log must reproduce every hash. See docs/design/platform.md. The wash. Jets are traced on the GPU from the nozzle positions measured on the machine and the turning of the arms, onto the exact shapes of the load. Splash and drips travel as droplets; water that lands runs down surfaces as a film, pools where a surface holds it and drains where it does not. A soil model per kind of soil then removes soil with time, temperature and the chemistry of the wash water (detergent, enzymes, bleach), over the whole programme. Where the water goes is cached apart from the soil and the chemistry, so a wash with other soil parameters replays in seconds to about a minute. The official tier works on blocks of 2 mm, the fast tier on 4 mm. See docs/design/scope.md for what is built and what is left out, and docs/design/sim-core.md for the design of the physics. The scoring. After the wash an inspector looks at every item. An item is clean when it carries at most 4 specks and 4 mm² of visible soil, counting what dirty water left where it stood on the item. Each item is worth a number of points stated on the level card; a clean item earns them, an item that is not clean or was left on the counter earns nothing. An episode is one load and one wash. The report also gives a graded score from 0 to 5 for each item and what is left where, which do not change the points. See docs/benchmark/README.md and docs/benchmark/levels.md. The calibration. Every physical constant of the wash is in a parameter registry with a default, a range and a source. A wash record describes a real test wash: the machine and the programme, each item with its soil and where it stood, and what was seen afterwards. The calibration tool runs the simulation on a record, scores it against what was seen, fits chosen parameters and says which parameters the data can and cannot identify. The first wash record is four egg-yolk plates on Eco 50. See docs/calibration/wash-record.md, docs/calibration/fitting.md and, for the set the game washes with, docs/calibration/anchoring-v7.md. Check the simulation yourself The phenomena suite (48 phenomena, 82 washes; about 15 minutes at the fast tier when nothing is cached, two and a half when everything is). Run these from the root of the repository, in a POSIX shell: INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts --list INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts P01 P36 --tier fast \ --out .spotless/phenomena INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts P36 --tier fast \ --params packages/calibration/anchors/anchored-v7.owner-capsule.json --dose-g 12.9 \ --out .spotless/phenomena With no ids it runs all 48. Without --params it washes with the registry defaults and the reference detergent; the third form washes as the game does, with the calibrated set and the capsule. The commands above send their reports to the git-ignored .spotless/phenomena. The default is packages/sim-verify/phenomena/reports/, which holds the stored reports of the project. The calibration tool, on the first test wash: pnpm --filter @spotless/calibration spotless-fit validate \ packages/calibration/records/owner/owner-wash-01-egg-yolk-eco50.measured.json pnpm --filter @spotless/calibration spotless-fit predict \ packages/calibration/records/owner/owner-wash-01-egg-yolk-eco50.measured.json \ --params packages/calibration/anchors/anchored-v7.owner-capsule.json validate checks a wash record; predict says what the simulation gives for every observation in it (five to seven minutes the first time, less once the water of the load is cached). With --params, predict washes as the game does; without it, it uses the registry defaults. Its warning that there is no calibration.json beside the set is expected. The saved loads against the loading physics: pnpm --filter @spotless/loader check-loads tutorial-careful pnpm --filter @spotless/loader check-loads --jobs 3 # all 25 of them: about 50 minutes Scope and limitations DishwasherBench models one machine and scores one programme, Eco 50, with one detergent. The wash is calibrated on a test wash of that machine (four egg-yolk plates) and on the published class means of a sister machine, the Bosch SMV6ECX51E. docs/validation/README.md has the full account, with every number and where it comes from. Three things decide most of a score: What is loaded. An item left on the counter earns nothing. Which way up the hollow pieces go. A glass, mug or pot left mouth up comes out not clean. About three quarters of the gap between a careful and a careless reference load is hollow pieces put in the wrong way up. Detergent and nesting. A blocked detergent tray leaves protein soils (egg, yoghurt, mince, milk) on the load, and a bowl or spoon that lies fully in another comes out not clean. The wash does not respond to how plates and cutlery are stacked: plates that lean on each other and cutlery crowded into one cell come out clean, where a real machine would be expected to leave soil. A score therefore does not show how well plates and cutlery were stacked (issue 1). Of the 48 loading phenomena in the suite, 17 pass. Drying, spots and film on glass, items moved by the jets and soil settling on clean pieces are outside the model (issue 7). The adapter for Anthropic's API is tested against a local stand-in only (issue 13). Open work is tracked as issues, each written as something a contributor could pick up, and docs/ROADMAP.md is the map of them. blocks.html_en: Loading. Every item and every part of the machine is a rigid compound of exact shapes generated from a parametric description; the picture, the collision shape and the surfaces the wash sees all come from that one description. Items are placed with rigid-body physics (Jolt) at a fixed step, with the player's inputs rounded to 1 mm and 1 degree, so that a person and a model act on the same grid and the same load always settles the same way. Every action is logged with a hash of the scene after it, and replaying the log must reproduce every hash. See docs/design/platform.md.

blocks.html_en: The wash. Jets are traced on the GPU from the nozzle positions measured on the machine and the turning of the arms, onto the exact shapes of the load. Splash and drips travel as droplets; water that lands runs down surfaces as a film, pools where a surface holds it and drains where it does not. A soil model per kind of soil then removes soil with time, temperature and the chemistry of the wash water (detergent, enzymes, bleach), over the whole programme. Where the water goes is cached apart from the soil and the chemistry, so a wash with other soil parameters replays in seconds to about a minute. The official tier works on blocks of 2 mm, the fast tier on 4 mm. See docs/design/scope.md for what is built and what is left out, and docs/design/sim-core.md for the design of the physics.

blocks.html_en: The scoring. After the wash an inspector looks at every item. An item is clean when it carries at most 4 specks and 4 mm² of visible soil, counting what dirty water left where it stood on the item. Each item is worth a number of points stated on the level card; a clean item earns them, an item that is not clean or was left on the counter earns nothing. An episode is one load and one wash. The report also gives a graded score from 0 to 5 for each item and what is left where, which do not change the points. See docs/benchmark/README.md and docs/benchmark/levels.md.

content_html_zh:
DishwasherBench is a dishwasher-loading game on a physical simulation of a real machine, built to benchmark language models and playable by people in a browser. The game inside is called Spotless, and the packages are named @spotless/*.

A player loads a 3D model of a Bosch SMV4HAX40G with rigid-body physics. A wash on its Eco 50 programme is then simulated (jets, droplets, run-off, soil and detergent chemistry), and the player gets points for every item that comes out clean. On every level after the first, not everything fits, so the player has to choose what to load and how.

  • Physical. Loading is rigid-body physics on exact shapes. The wash traces water from the nozzle positions measured on the machine and is calibrated on a test wash of it.
  • Deterministic and verifiable. The same load always settles the same way, and every episode is a record that anyone can verify by replaying it and by washing its load again.
  • One game for people and models. People play in a browser and models play through MCP, with the same actions on the same grid.

特征

  • The machine. A Bosch SMV4HAX40G as data and geometry, from photographs and tape readings of the real machine (packages/machine): both baskets with their tine rows, shelves and rests, the spray arms and the Eco 50 programme.
  • Loading. A catalogue of items and soils, deterministic rigid-body loading (Jolt), and a session layer with the actions and queries of the game (place, remove, set_rack, list_slots, check_load and the rest).
  • The wash. A simulation at two tiers: the official tier gives the scored result, and the fast tier a preview in about a minute. An official wash of the largest level takes about five minutes on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Pro).
  • A course of seven levels, numbered in order of difficulty (docs/benchmark/levels.md), each with saved reference loads of three scripted players (careful, careless, random).
  • Three ways to play. The page (apps/web), an MCP server for agents (packages/mcp), and a harness that runs scripted players and models and writes verified episode records (packages/bench).
  • 检查。 48 loading phenomena from the literature as executable pairs of washes (docs/research/standards.md section 9), and a calibration tool that scores the simulation against a record of a real wash, fits parameters and ranks candidate test washes.

要求

  • macOS. Developed and tested on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Pro, 18 GB) under macOS 27, where every figure in this repository was measured. Linux and Windows are untested (issue 28).
  • Node 20.19 or newer in the 20 line (.nvmrc pins 20.19.0; an older Node is refused at install), and pnpm 9 (package.json names 9.4.0; corepack enable picks it up).
  • A GPU that Dawn can open. The wash traces water on the GPU through WebGPU from Node (the webgpu package, version 0.6.2, which carries prebuilt Dawn binaries). On a Mac that is Metal. Version 0.6.2 loads on macOS 27 and does not load on macOS 14.7.
  • Google Chrome or Chromium, for the pictures an agent is sent and for the scripts that drive the page. The harness looks for it in the usual install locations; set SPOTLESS_CHROME to the path of the program to choose another. Playing by hand needs only a desktop browser, and scripted players need none (--no-render).
  • Disk and memory. About 680 MB for the clone (a download of about 290 MB) and about 420 MB for node_modules; 1 to 2 GB of memory for an official wash of a level.
  • Ports 8787 (game server) and 8788 (MCP server), or others of your choosing.

Results are repeatable bit for bit on one machine, and every result names the stack it was computed on: across machines, operating-system builds and versions of the webgpu package, results can differ in the last bits (docs/research/spike-gpu-compute-macos27-recheck.md).

快速启动

git clone https://github.com/composo-ai/DishwasherBench.git
cd DishwasherBench
corepack enable                       # once: makes pnpm 9.4.0 available
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile        # about 15 seconds the first time

There is no build step for the packages: they are consumed as TypeScript source and run with tsx. Only the page is built, by the play command below.

Wash a saved load from the command line:

pnpm --filter @spotless/wash-runner wash-load tutorial-careful --tier fast       # under a minute
pnpm --filter @spotless/wash-runner wash-load tutorial-careful --tier official   # about 5 minutes the first time

It prints the points and, for each item, the verdict, the score and what is left on it. The saved loads are in packages/loader/loads/ (<level>-<player>.json). The first wash of a load works out where the water goes and keeps that in .spotless/exposure-cache, so a second wash of the same load takes seconds to about a minute (pass --no-cache to switch this off).

运行检查：

pnpm typecheck      # the root and every package; a few seconds
pnpm test           # every package; 8 to 17 minutes, with real washes on the GPU

A wash is tied to its parameter set. The set the game washes with (anchored-v7.owner-capsule, in packages/calibration/anchors/) records the state of the simulation source and of the machine data it was made for. After a change to either, the wash stops and lists what differs. CONTRIBUTING.md explains the rule and how to make the set current again.

Play in the browser

pnpm --filter @spotless/web play

This builds the page and starts the game server. Open http://127.0.0.1:8787 (add --port <n> for another port). The page plays music; the Sound button turns it off.

When you start the wash you choose between two kinds:

  • Quick preview: the fast tier, in about a minute.
  • Full wash: the official tier, in several minutes. This is the scored result, and the report of a preview offers it on the same load.

The game is scored on Eco 50 with one capsule of detergent (Finish Powerball Ultimate, 12.9 g). The levels are listed 1 to 7 in order of difficulty.

Plates, bowls and cutlery are placed by pointing. For a tight spot, such as a plate beside one already placed or a cup against the side rests of the upper basket, pick the piece up and press "Suggest spots" (it costs one query), then click a numbered mark.

The server answers the page it serves and clients on your own machine. --allow-origin admits a page served from another origin, and --allow-host a request under another host name (SECURITY.md).

After a quick preview of a deliberately careless load of the first level: a bowl left mouth up holds 432 ml of water and is not clean, and the report says that a fork held the lower spray arm still.

Looking closely at one item after the wash: the residue is painted where it was left, with its area and the water the item held.

Run a scripted player

A scripted player needs no model and costs nothing. This plays the first level with the careful reference player at the official tier, then verifies the record by replaying its actions and by washing the load a second time (about five minutes each):

pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies careful \
  --no-render --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/scripted"
pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench verify \
  "$PWD"/.spotless/bench/scripted/tutorial__careful__*/record.json --rewash
  • Give --out as an absolute path; a relative one resolves inside packages/bench.
  • The scripted players are empty, random, careless and careful. Add --tier fast for a preview in about a minute; the record and the results table label it as a preview.
  • Each run writes under --out: record.json, a results table (results.md, results.json), the data of the game server it started (server-data/) and, without --no-render, the pictures the tools returned.

The scripted careful player's load of the largest level (62 pieces on the counter, 49 loaded), from above and from the front and side. Both models that have played beat it.

Run a model

Everything about the harness, what each kind of player sees and what is recorded is in docs/benchmark/README.md.

A model run costs money. Copy .env.example to .env (which git ignores) and fill in the address and the key of your endpoint. The command prints the names of the variables it set, never a value, and neither the key nor the address is written to a record.

A model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenAI, Azure, or any server with the Responses or chat completions API):

pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies openai:gpt-6.1-sol \
  --max-input-tokens 2000000 --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/sol-tutorial"
  • The policy names the model or, on Azure, the deployment: openai:<model or deployment>.
  • --max-input-tokens ends an episode before its requests add up to more. The first level takes 0.4 to 0.65 million input tokens, a level of 37 pieces 2.5 to 2.8 million, and the largest level (62 pieces) 3.0 to 3.2 million, with 95 % or more of it read from the provider's cache. Use limits of 2,000,000, 12,000,000 and 20,000,000.
  • The harness records tokens, and a cost when prices are given in .env.
  • The wash is at the official tier, which is the score; --tier fast gives a preview.
  • Each run writes the record, the transcript, the pictures and a results table under --out, and verifies the episode by replaying its action log.
  • With no address set, no request is made and the command exits with status 1.

A model through Anthropic's API, with the key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (put the model's id in place of <model id>):

pnpm --filter @spotless/bench bench run --levels tutorial --policies anthropic:<model id> \
  --max-input-tokens 2000000 --out "$PWD/.spotless/bench/anthropic-tutorial"

The SDK also accepts a stored login profile, so a run can spend without a key in .env.

连接 MCP 客户端

Any agent that speaks MCP can play. An MCP server is bound to one episode, so start the game server in benchmark mode and create the episode first.

# 1. The game server (the token: 8 characters or more, of your choosing)
pnpm --filter @spotless/server exec tsx src/cli.ts serve --admin-token <token> --wash-tier fast \
  --data "$PWD/.spotless"

# 2. An episode; prints an address for the page, and the episode's id
pnpm --filter @spotless/server exec tsx src/cli.ts link --admin-token <token> \
  --level tutorial --player my-agent --agent

# 3. For a client that speaks streamable HTTP: serves http://127.0.0.1:8788/mcp
pnpm --filter @spotless/mcp exec tsx src/cli.ts --server http://127.0.0.1:8787 \
  --session <episode id> --http --port 8788

--data keeps the server's files, the episode records among them (.spotless/episodes/), in the directory the page uses; without it serve writes to packages/server/.spotless. The address that link prints shows the episode in the page once the page has been built (pnpm --filter @spotless/web build, which play also does). If the game server is on another port (serve --port <n>), give link its address with --server http://127.0.0.1:<n>. For a desktop client that starts the MCP server itself over stdio, the configuration is in docs/benchmark/README.md section 3.

The agent gets thirteen tools (place, remove, reset, set_rack, start_cycle, get_level, get_item, get_state, render, preview, list_slots, check_load, get_report). To try one call by hand:

pnpm --filter @spotless/mcp exec tsx scripts/call.ts --url http://127.0.0.1:8788/mcp get_state '{}'

Both servers listen on 127.0.0.1 and serve clients on your own machine. For a client that reaches them under another name, for example from a container, start them with --allow-host <name> (SECURITY.md).

它是如何运作的

Loading. Every item and every part of the machine is a rigid compound of exact shapes generated from a parametric description; the picture, the collision shape and the surfaces the wash sees all come from that one description. Items are placed with rigid-body physics (Jolt) at a fixed step, with the player's inputs rounded to 1 mm and 1 degree, so that a person and a model act on the same grid and the same load always settles the same way. Every action is logged with a hash of the scene after it, and replaying the log must reproduce every hash. See docs/design/platform.md.

The wash. Jets are traced on the GPU from the nozzle positions measured on the machine and the turning of the arms, onto the exact shapes of the load. Splash and drips travel as droplets; water that lands runs down surfaces as a film, pools where a surface holds it and drains where it does not. A soil model per kind of soil then removes soil with time, temperature and the chemistry of the wash water (detergent, enzymes, bleach), over the whole programme. Where the water goes is cached apart from the soil and the chemistry, so a wash with other soil parameters replays in seconds to about a minute. The official tier works on blocks of 2 mm, the fast tier on 4 mm. See docs/design/scope.md for what is built and what is left out, and docs/design/sim-core.md for the design of the physics.

The scoring. After the wash an inspector looks at every item. An item is clean when it carries at most 4 specks and 4 mm² of visible soil, counting what dirty water left where it stood on the item. Each item is worth a number of points stated on the level card; a clean item earns them, an item that is not clean or was left on the counter earns nothing. An episode is one load and one wash. The report also gives a graded score from 0 to 5 for each item and what is left where, which do not change the points. See docs/benchmark/README.md and docs/benchmark/levels.md.

The calibration. Every physical constant of the wash is in a parameter registry with a default, a range and a source. A wash record describes a real test wash: the machine and the programme, each item with its soil and where it stood, and what was seen afterwards. The calibration tool runs the simulation on a record, scores it against what was seen, fits chosen parameters and says which parameters the data can and cannot identify. The first wash record is four egg-yolk plates on Eco 50. See docs/calibration/wash-record.md, docs/calibration/fitting.md and, for the set the game washes with, docs/calibration/anchoring-v7.md.

Check the simulation yourself

The phenomena suite (48 phenomena, 82 washes; about 15 minutes at the fast tier when nothing is cached, two and a half when everything is). Run these from the root of the repository, in a POSIX shell:

INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts --list
INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts P01 P36 --tier fast \
  --out .spotless/phenomena
INIT_CWD=. pnpm exec tsx packages/sim-verify/src/phenomena/cli.ts P36 --tier fast \
  --params packages/calibration/anchors/anchored-v7.owner-capsule.json --dose-g 12.9 \
  --out .spotless/phenomena

With no ids it runs all 48. Without --params it washes with the registry defaults and the reference detergent; the third form washes as the game does, with the calibrated set and the capsule. The commands above send their reports to the git-ignored .spotless/phenomena. The default is packages/sim-verify/phenomena/reports/, which holds the stored reports of the project.

The calibration tool, on the first test wash:

pnpm --filter @spotless/calibration spotless-fit validate \
  packages/calibration/records/owner/owner-wash-01-egg-yolk-eco50.measured.json
pnpm --filter @spotless/calibration spotless-fit predict \
  packages/calibration/records/owner/owner-wash-01-egg-yolk-eco50.measured.json \
  --params packages/calibration/anchors/anchored-v7.owner-capsule.json

validate checks a wash record; predict says what the simulation gives for every observation in it (five to seven minutes the first time, less once the water of the load is cached). With --params, predict washes as the game does; without it, it uses the registry defaults. Its warning that there is no calibration.json beside the set is expected.

The saved loads against the loading physics:

pnpm --filter @spotless/loader check-loads tutorial-careful
pnpm --filter @spotless/loader check-loads --jobs 3      # all 25 of them: about 50 minutes

范围和限制

DishwasherBench models one machine and scores one programme, Eco 50, with one detergent. The wash is calibrated on a test wash of that machine (four egg-yolk plates) and on the published class means of a sister machine, the Bosch SMV6ECX51E. docs/validation/README.md has the full account, with every number and where it comes from.

Three things decide most of a score:

  • What is loaded. An item left on the counter earns nothing.
  • Which way up the hollow pieces go. A glass, mug or pot left mouth up comes out not clean. About three quarters of the gap between a careful and a careless reference load is hollow pieces put in the wrong way up.
  • Detergent and nesting. A blocked detergent tray leaves protein soils (egg, yoghurt, mince, milk) on the load, and a bowl or spoon that lies fully in another comes out not clean.

The wash does not respond to how plates and cutlery are stacked: plates that lean on each other and cutlery crowded into one cell come out clean, where a real machine would be expected to leave soil. A score therefore does not show how well plates and cutlery were stacked (issue 1). Of the 48 loading phenomena in the suite, 17 pass. Drying, spots and film on glass, items moved by the jets and soil settling on clean pieces are outside the model (issue 7). The adapter for Anthropic's API is tested against a local stand-in only (issue 13).

Open work is tracked as issues, each written as something a contributor could pick up, and docs/ROADMAP.md is the map of them.
